Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced ITU-sourced bandwidth data via aggregators rather than confirming a genuine unknown, so the row was moved to the full path. TheGlobalEconomy.com (citing ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicators) records Benin at 2.84 kbit/s per internet user in 2016, the latest year in that series; the USAID Digital Development site separately lists international bandwidth per user at 1.66 (page dated 2023, underlying year unclear). No more recent ITU figure was located despite searching. Both readings sit well within the "Very Low" band (<5 kbit/s per user), supporting Value Code 1 rather than the original 0/Unknown. Flagged for human review because the only located data point is nearly a decade old and a fresher ITU figure may exist that a targeted ITU-database lookup could surface.
revised_comments: Benin's international internet bandwidth per internet user is very low. ITU World Telecommunication/ICT Indicator data (as reported by TheGlobalEconomy.com) place Benin at 2.84 kbit/s per user in 2016, the most recent year available in that series, while a separate aggregator estimate puts the figure at around 1.66 kbit/s per user. Both readings fall well below the 5 kbit/s per user threshold, reflecting limited international connectivity capacity relative to the size of the internet-using population.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced a clearly authoritative, current source (Packet Clearing House IXP directory and Internet Society Pulse IXP tracker), so the row was moved to the full path. Benin IX (Benin-IX), established December 2013 in Cotonou, is confirmed active in PCH's global IXP directory; the Internet Society's Pulse tracker (PeeringDB-sourced member data, current to January 2026) shows a small number of active local participants (including ISOCEL SA and the state-owned Société Béninoise d'Infrastructures Numériques) alongside Packet Clearing House peering nodes. This is a single, active IXP with limited local participation, supporting Value Code 3 rather than the original 0/Unknown.
revised_comments: Benin has a single operational Internet Exchange Point, Benin-IX, established in December 2013 and based in Cotonou. Current tracking by the Internet Society's Pulse IXP tracker and Packet Clearing House's global IXP directory confirms it remains active, though participation is limited to a small number of local networks (including ISOCEL SA and the state-owned Société Béninoise d'Infrastructures Numériques) alongside international peering nodes.

Definition: Whether the government has established dedicated data center infrastructure and/or a government cloud (G-Cloud) strategy for hosting e-government services and public sector data domestically. Critical for data sovereignty and e-government service delivery.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced clearly authoritative government and trade-press sources, so the row was moved to the full path. Benin operates a national data centre (built to Tier 3/ANSI-TIA-942 standard) in Abomey-Calavi, which began technical testing in 2021 and was described as Benin's "first Tier 3 datacentre" by the Director-General of the Agency for Digital Development in a 2024 interview; it is run by state operator SBIM. The National Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Strategy (SNIAM 2023-2027), adopted by the Council of Ministers in January 2023, explicitly plans to build government cloud/AI-as-a-service capability on top of this data centre. A June 2026 DataCenterDynamics report confirms a World Bank-funded feasibility study is under way for a second, redundant national data centre. This combination of an operational national data centre plus an adopted cloud/data strategy supports Value Code 4 rather than the original 0/Unknown.
revised_comments: Benin operates a national data centre in Abomey-Calavi, built to Tier 3 (ANSI/TIA-942) standard and run by the state telecoms operator SBIM; it has been operational since around 2021. The government's National Artificial Intelligence and Big Data Strategy (SNIAM 2023-2027), adopted in January 2023, sets out plans to equip this data centre with cloud and AI-as-a-service capability for hosting public-sector systems. A World Bank-funded feasibility study for a second, redundant national data centre was under way as of mid-2026, indicating continued investment in domestic government hosting infrastructure.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced tariff and income data, so the row was moved to the full path, but the evidence does not resolve cleanly to a single Value Code. Reported residential tariffs vary by source and consumption band: a World Bank tariff-design survey (2015-16 data) documents an increasing-block tariff starting around USD 0.16/kWh for the lowest band (0-20 kWh) rising to USD 0.22-0.23/kWh above that; a 2025 academic study citing IFC (2023a) instead reports an average retail tariff of USD 0.25/kWh in 2021. Benin's GNI per capita, Atlas method, was USD 1,390 (2023) / USD 1,430 (2024), i.e. roughly USD 116-119/month. Depending on the assumed basic consumption level (20-50 kWh/month), the bill-to-income ratio ranges from around 3% to 11% of monthly GNI per capita, spanning three different bands on the Value Code scale (3, 2, and 1). No single authoritative electricity-affordability index (e.g. RISE, A4AI) with a definitive Benin score was found. Given this genuine ambiguity, the code is left blank for human review rather than guessed.
revised_comments: Benin's residential electricity tariffs follow an increasing block structure, with published rates ranging from around USD 0.16 per kWh for the lowest consumption band to approximately USD 0.25 per kWh at typical retail levels (2021-based estimates). Gross national income per capita (Atlas method) stood at USD 1,390-1,430 in 2023-24, equivalent to roughly USD 116-119 per month. Electricity affordability for an average household therefore varies considerably depending on assumed consumption levels, and no single authoritative affordability index score specific to Benin was identified.

Comments: No data found after thorough searching

revision_notes: Light check surfaced clear World Bank/IEA data, so the row was moved to the full path. World Bank WDI indicator EG.ELC.RNEW.ZS (sourced from the IEA) records Benin's renewable electricity output at 0.26% of total electricity output in 2021, the most recent year available, down from 0.55% in 2020. This is far below the 10% threshold for Value Code 2, supporting Value Code 1 (<10%) rather than the original 0/Unknown. Note this reflects Benin's domestic generation mix only; Benin imports a large share of its electricity (around 75% in 2019, per IFC) from neighbouring countries' hydropower, which is not captured by this domestic-generation indicator.
revised_comments: Renewable sources contribute a very small share of Benin's domestic electricity generation. World Bank data (sourced from the IEA) records renewable electricity output at 0.26% of total electricity output in 2021, the latest year available, continuing a long-term pattern of minimal domestic renewable generation (the indicator has not exceeded 3.4% since 1990). Benin relies heavily on imported electricity, including hydropower from neighbouring countries, which is not reflected in this domestic generation-mix indicator.

Definition: The scale and quality of tertiary-level ICT and STEM education programmes available in the country, based on the number and quality of institutions offering ICT degrees, computer science programmes, and engineering courses relative to the population.
Comments: No data found after thorough searching
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced UNESCO UIS/World Bank graduate-share data and clear evidence of a broad institutional base, so the row was moved to the full path. UNESCO UIS data (via World Bank/Trading Economics) records 11.34% of Benin's tertiary graduates in Natural Sciences, Mathematics and Statistics programmes in 2018 (most recent year located); this excludes engineering and ICT-specific graduates, so the total STEM share is likely higher. Benin has a dedicated national STIM university (UNSTIM, established 2016, with multiple campuses), a long-standing specialist computing institute (IFRI, Institut de Formation et de Recherche en Informatique, at the University of Abomey-Calavi), an engineering faculty (EPAC) at the same university, and a newly launched engineering/data-science institute (Sèmè City Institute of Technology and Innovation, developed in partnership with France's Centrale Group). Dozens of private institutions across several cities (Cotonou, Calavi, Porto-Novo, Parakou, Bohicon, Natitingou) also offer computer science, telecoms and IT degrees. This breadth of established, diversified institutions supports Value Code 4 (Good) rather than the original 0/Unknown, though no ranking evidence (e.g. QS by subject) of regional reputation was found to justify Code 5.
revised_comments: Benin has an established and diversifying tertiary ICT/STEM education base. UNESCO UIS data record around 11% of tertiary graduates completing Natural Sciences, Mathematics and Statistics programmes (2018, most recent year available), a figure that excludes engineering and computing graduates and so understates total STEM output. The country has a dedicated national STIM university (Université Nationale des Sciences, Technologies, Ingénierie et Mathématiques, UNSTIM, established 2016, with campuses in several towns), a long-standing specialist computing institute (IFRI) within the University of Abomey-Calavi, an engineering faculty (EPAC), and a newly launched engineering and data-science institute, the Sèmè City Institute of Technology and Innovation, developed in partnership with France's Centrale Group. Dozens of additional private institutions across Cotonou, Calavi, Porto-Novo, Parakou and other cities offer computer science, telecommunications and IT degree programmes, indicating a moderately mature and expanding ecosystem, though without international ranking recognition.
